facts.claim: Coyle describes myelin as the fatty insulation around neurons; like insulation on wiring, more of it lets signals travel faster and more accurately. 'Practice makes myelin, and myelin makes perfect.'
facts.source: retinart summary; Substack preview quoting the opening; Shortform

facts.claim: Myelin is living tissue, grows, and is not fixed at birth; it builds when a specific circuit fires repeatedly.

Starting in December 2006 Coyle visited nine small 'talent hotbeds' (chicken-wire Harvards), among them a tennis court in Moscow, a soccer field in Sao Paulo, a vocal studio in Dallas, a school in San Jose and a baseball island in the Caribbean. He noticed players alternating between fluent, fast movement and slow, halting struggle.
In Sao Paulo, 11-year-old Brunio fails at a ball-handling move called the elastico, slows it down, breaks it into parts, and then 'something clicks'.
In Dallas, Jennie (24) rehearses the chorus of 'Running Out of Time', stopping at each miss, and gets the measure right on the sixth try.

Deep practice: struggling in certain targeted ways at the edge of current ability, in a 'sweet spot' where reach exceeds grasp. Mistakes, and attention to them, are part of how the circuit fires better. Coyle's paradox: the struggle makes you smarter.

Futsal: small heavy ball, fewer players, small court. Players touch the ball about six times more per minute than in outdoor soccer, per a Liverpool University study cited in the excerpt. Juninho did not play on a full-size grass pitch until he was 14. Dr. Emilio Miranda: 'No time plus no space equals better skills.'
Coyle claims specific kinds of practice build skill up to ten times faster than conventional practice.

Coyle's three elements: deep practice, ignition, master coaching. He defines talent narrowly as repeatable skills that do not depend on physical size. 'Although talent feels and looks predestined, in fact we have a good deal of control over what skills we develop.'
